article_title: Roadblocks and Routes: Professional Development in Math in Common Districts
citation: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). Roadblocks and routes: Professional development in Math in Common districts. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org/permissions
title: Develop an array of differentiated PD strategies rather than one-size-fits-all PD
description: Based on five years of observations, the report recommends that districts "Develop an array of PD strategies for differentiating in-service support, to enable useful learning for all teachers," following multiple routes rather than one-size-fits-all PD. Because teachers' prior experience and training may not prepare them for standards implementation, districts should organize many different PD formats and experiences reflecting the diverse ways people learn.
requirements: Funding or reallocated resources to support multiple PD formats and teachers' collaborative work
constraints: The report notes large pull-out PD days can default to a sit-and-get model disconnected from daily classroom work, and out-of-contract-time PD suffered sub-optimal attendance
target_learners: K–8 mathematics teachers with diverse prior experience and training
target_learning_goals: Effective implementation of new mathematics standards
examples: MiC districts used summer institutes, after-school trainings, book studies, lesson study, site-based PLCs, online repositories and PD modules, and coaching, differentiating by teacher needs
key_sources: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). Roadblocks and routes: Professional development in Math in Common districts. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org/permissions

article_title: How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Texas Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://EdTrust.org
title: Alliance for Resource Equity (ARE) diagnostic toolkit organized around ten dimensions of equity
description: The Alliance for Resource Equity, a partnership between Ed Trust and Education Resource Strategies, categorizes the student experience into 10 "dimensions of equity." Its toolkit includes a diagnostic tool organized around "key questions" for identifying problem areas, plus practical guidebooks offering actions to address them. The brief highlights relevant key questions under each SEAD policy section for district leaders and advocates.
requirements: District leaders and advocates to use the diagnostic key questions and guidebooks at the local level
target_learners: District leaders and advocates working to improve local policies and practices
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing and addressing equity problems in the student experience
examples: Each policy section of the brief closes with ARE key questions, such as whether each student experiences a safe school with transparent, consistently enforced rules and discipline policies

article_title: BEAGLE: Behavior-Enforced Agent for Grounded Learner Emulation
citation: Hanchen David Wang, Clayton Cohn, Zifan Xu, Siyuan Guo, Gautam Biswas, Meiyi Ma. (2026). BEAGLE: Behavior-Enforced Agent for Grounded Learner Emulation. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13280
title: Enforce novice-like simulation architecturally rather than through prompting or context engineering
description: The article's central design recommendation is that realistic synthetic student behavior cannot be elicited from preference-tuned LLMs by persona prompting or context injection alone; it requires architectural enforcement. Symbolic control (semi-Markov dynamics, BKT with flaw injection) and a decoupled Strategist/Executor constrain what the model can do, so that "sequence-level student simulation cannot be recovered through context engineering alone; architectural enforcement closes the gap." The +M baseline variants, which inject BEAGLE's metacognitive vocabulary without the architecture, empirically isolate prompt effects from architectural ones.
requirements: A calibrated symbolic-control layer (semi-Markov transitions and Gamma durations fit on historical student logs) plus a knowledge model with explicit flaw injection
constraints: +M variants never beat DKL = 0.63 or Realism = 1.64, and removing the semi-Markov controller while preserving prompts pushes DKL to 6.81
target_learners: researchers and builders of adaptive tutoring systems and pedagogical agents needing synthetic novice data
target_learning_goals: generation of high-fidelity synthetic learner trajectories for training tutors and stress-testing pedagogical interventions
examples: BEAGLE implements the principle via three mechanisms: semi-Markov behavior control, BKT+EFI knowledge constraints, and the Strategist/Executor split with observation filtering
key_sources: Hanchen David Wang, Clayton Cohn, Zifan Xu, Siyuan Guo, Gautam Biswas, Meiyi Ma. (2026). BEAGLE: Behavior-Enforced Agent for Grounded Learner Emulation. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13280

article_title: Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K-12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools
citation: Jacobson, M. J.; Rodriguez-Rivera, G.; Drineas, P.; and Xue, Y. (2026). Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K–12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18072
title: ARC: a hubs-based K–12 AI and robotics education framework with a self-reinforcing mentorship loop
description: ARC organizes hands-on, mentor-led workshop events around regional hubs: primary hubs at colleges train undergraduate mentors via a credit-bearing course and host workshops for nearby K–12 teams, and mature school programs become secondary hubs that host workshops for other nearby schools. The article describes "a self-reinforcing education loop" in which primary hubs train undergraduates, undergraduates teach K–12 students, teams become self-sustaining, and mature teams host their own workshops, giving the framework potential for multiplicative and super-linear growth in mentorship capacity and geographic reach. Workshop content is adapted to age, experience, and competition level, from foundational programming for FLL teams to autonomy, computer vision, and AI for advanced teams.
requirements: Primary hubs require colleges or other STEM institutions able to run the ARC course, train undergraduate mentors, and host workshops; secondary hubs require a mature, self-sustaining school program with enough internal technical knowledge to help nearby teams.
constraints: The trial did not test the full regional system, which would require several years for supported programs to mature and new hubs to form.
target_learners: K–12 students in rural and under-served regions
examples: The trial deployment at one large Indiana university enrolled nine undergraduates, ran weekly two-hour sessions, and supported three new FLL teams from one rural school using LEGO robots and two provided FLL game arenas.
key_sources: Jacobson, M. J.; Rodriguez-Rivera, G.; Drineas, P.; and Xue, Y. (2026). Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K–12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18072

article_title: Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K-12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools
citation: Jacobson, M. J.; Rodriguez-Rivera, G.; Drineas, P.; and Xue, Y. (2026). Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K–12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18072
title: Spatially-explicit Markov model of ARC regional growth
description: A discrete-time stochastic model with annual transitions representing both school robotics-program development and each school's relationship to the ARC network. Each K–12 school carries two state variables — a FIRST program state (no program, Early, Mature) and an ARC state (Unreachable, Reachable, Supported, secondary Hub) — with nine legal combinations, plus college hub states; geography enters through a fixed relation specifying which schools each hub can serve. The article states "Reachability alone does not alter a school's natural program-development probabilities" and that direct ARC support is what allows different maturation and persistence behavior. It was instantiated for Indiana with 1,925 public K–12 schools and 32 potential college hubs, simulated 40 years over 1,000 Monte Carlo runs across 12 optimism levels, with ablations isolating hub-growth mechanisms.
requirements: A run requires the set of schools, initial valid states, potential primary-hub colleges, the geographic relation, model parameters, and rules for selecting schools when launch or support capacity is limited.
constraints: A mean-field approximation replacing exact geography with regional averages is more analytically tractable but loses spatial clustering, overlapping coverage, and local capacity constraints.
target_learners: K–12 schools in a mixed-rural region being modeled
target_learning_goals: projecting regional growth of robotics program access and mentorship reach
examples: At optimism level 6 the model produced 992 programs and reached 1,415 schools after 40 years, compared with a mean of 161 programs under the ARC-off natural-growth baseline.
key_sources: Jacobson, M. J.; Rodriguez-Rivera, G.; Drineas, P.; and Xue, Y. (2026). Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K–12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18072

article_title: Argus: Academic Integrity in the Era of Generative AI
citation: David Racovan, Ajay Rawat, Christopher K. May, Jeffrey A. Turkstra. (2026). Argus: Academic Integrity in the Era of Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36073
title: Argus: a static-analysis triage tool for detecting LLM-assisted code development
description: Argus is a static analysis system that processes each student's Git repository commit history, evaluating heuristic indicators in two categories: "Advanced C topics not taught in the course curriculum" and "stylistic patterns inconsistent with course conventions". Weighted indicators, temporal span analysis, and burst detection (commits of at least 30 new lines at 15 or more lines per minute) combine into an aggregate H-score, with dynamic normalization attenuating indicators common in the class. Scores surface through a web interface ranking students for staff review.
requirements: Requires access to the student's working history, such as automatic Git commits on a university-managed server; at institutions without similar infrastructure it may still function on static heuristic indicators alone.
constraints: A high H-score is never treated as evidence of misconduct; benign behaviors such as prior programming experience or drafting in an external editor can produce elevated scores.
target_learners: undergraduate students in large-enrollment introductory C programming (CS2) courses
examples: In Spring 2026, three course staff reviewed the top 300 students by H-score in roughly 8 hours each, with a median review time of about 1.5 minutes per student.
key_sources: David Racovan, Ajay Rawat, Christopher K. May, Jeffrey A. Turkstra. (2026). Argus: Academic Integrity in the Era of Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36073

article_title: CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy
citation: Dawei Xie, Khalil Anderson, Tochukwu Eze, Chenghong Lin, Bookyung Shin, and Marcelo Worsley. (2026). CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17259
title: LLM-generated artifacts serving dual roles as user-facing scaffolds and indexed retrieval infrastructure
description: A design pattern in which a first LLM pass produces structured analytical representations (concept maps, collaboration assessments) that are simultaneously visualized for human interpretation and indexed as the knowledge base a second agentic pass retrieves and reasons over. The article states that "the system is creating its own retrieval infrastructure: the artifacts generated in the first pass become the indexed knowledge that supports reasoning in the second pass". The artifacts offload identifying what matters and distilling it into analytical structures, letting the agent focus on synthesis and interpretation.
requirements: Artifacts must fall within the embedding model's context window (8,192 tokens, so no chunking was needed) and be indexed in collections separated by artifact type
constraints: Whether more open-ended or less formalized representations would provide the same retrieval advantage is stated to be an open question
target_learners: Learners and educators using AI-augmented analytics dashboards
target_learning_goals: Making collaboration visible and discussable; supporting grounded AI reasoning about group work
examples: CLARA indexes each artifact as a single document in its own ChromaDB collection, letting users restrict which representations the agent consults
key_sources: Dawei Xie, Khalil Anderson, Tochukwu Eze, Chenghong Lin, Bookyung Shin, and Marcelo Worsley. (2026). CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17259

article_title: ARPG+: a simulation-based study of real-time coaching for educational LLM prompting
citation: Ye, P.-G., Mo, K., Long, Y., Liu, M., Sang, H., & Zheng, J. (2026). ARPG+: a simulation-based study of real-time coaching for educational LLM prompting. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00606-9
title: ARPG+ dual-process real-time coaching system
description: ARPG+ is a hierarchical real-time coaching system coupling "a lightweight fast path with selectively triggered deep analysis under explicit latency budgets." A unified trigger variable combines abrupt quality shifts, sustained struggle, safety concerns, and scheduled probes into one decision. The system senses prompt drafts, conversation history, and telemetry; interprets them through cognitive load, ZPD, and metacognitive lenses; decides between fast-path and deep-path interventions; and acts with adaptive type, granularity, and intensity. Latency budgets are 50 ms for the fast path and 300 ms for the deep path.
requirements: A dual-model architecture separating behavior generation from independent evaluation; calibrated hyperparameters including overload tolerance ρ = 0.7 and ZPD multiplier κ = 1.5.
constraints: Evaluated only with LLM-based simulated learners; the authors state this is evidence of system feasibility and simulation-based performance, not educational effectiveness.
target_learners: Novice to advanced LLM users in educational settings
examples: Most turns finish on the fast path within budget; the deep path is reserved for moments that are difficult, risky, or diagnostically valuable.
key_sources: Ye, P.-G., Mo, K., Long, Y., Liu, M., Sang, H., & Zheng, J. (2026). ARPG+: a simulation-based study of real-time coaching for educational LLM prompting. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00606-9

article_title: Self-Determination and Positive Adult Outcomes: A Follow-up Study of Youth with Mental Retardation or Learning Disabilities
citation: Michael Wehmeyer, Michelle Schwartz. (1997). Self-Determination and Positive Adult Outcomes: A Follow-Up Study of Youth with Mental Retardation or Learning Disabilities. Exceptional Children, 63(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Self-Determination+and+Positive+Adult+Outcomes+Wehmeyer+Schwartz
title: The Arc's Self-Determination Scale
description: A 72-item self-report scale for adolescents with cognitive disabilities that operationalizes the four-essential-characteristics definitional framework. Completion of the scale provides data on student global self-determination, as well as individual autonomy, self-regulation, psychological empowerment, and self-realization. There are a total of 148 points available on the Scale and higher scores reflect higher self-determination. It was normed with 500 students with and without cognitive disabilities in rural, urban, and suburban districts in five states.
requirements: Designed for group or individual administration by classroom teachers and requires limited information to administer
constraints: The article notes concurrent criterion-related validity was established and adequate construct validity including factorial validity, but the measure is a self-report instrument
target_learning_goals: measuring self-determination as an educational outcome
examples: Used with 80 students with mental retardation or learning disabilities in their final high school year in Virginia, Connecticut, Alabama, and Texas

article_title: Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education
citation: Rivas SF, Saiz C and Ossa C (2022) Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education. Front. Psychol. 13:913219. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.913219
title: ARDESOS-DIAPROVE program: a 16-week critical thinking intervention integrating PBL and cooperative learning
description: ARDESOS-DIAPROVE (third version) is a classroom program that directly teaches critical thinking skills via Problem-Based Learning and cooperative learning. "The intervention took place over 16 weeks and is designed to be applied in classrooms over a timeframe of 55–60 h" in classes of around 30–35 students divided into groups of four, organized into six activity blocks (nature of critical thinking; problem-solving and effectiveness; explanation and causality; deduction and explanation; argumentation and deduction; problem-solving and decision-making). Tasks use common situations and professional/personal problems, with rubrics for every task and feedback in all sessions.
requirements: Instructors with training and good experience in the program
Tasks contextualized within everyday problems so students perceive skills as useful
constraints: DIAPROVE methodology adds observation development, combined use of facts and deduction, and management of de-confirmation procedures as its foundation
examples: Evaluation used the PENCRISAL test administered over the Internet via the SelectSurvey.NET V5 platform and the 52-item MAI, with measurements one week before and one week after the intervention.
key_sources: Rivas SF, Saiz C and Ossa C (2022) Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education. Front. Psychol. 13:913219. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.913219

article_title: Mathematics anxiety in children with developmental dyscalculia
citation: Rubinsten O, Tannock R. (2010). Mathematics anxiety in children with developmental dyscalculia. Behavioral and Brain Functions 6:46. http://www.behavioralandbrainfunctions.com/content/6/1/46
title: Arithmetic-affective priming task as an indirect measure of math anxiety
description: A novel computerized priming task in which single-digit arithmetic equations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) are preceded by one of four prime word types (positive, neutral, negative, mathematics-related) at a 250 ms stimulus onset asynchrony; participants judge as quickly as possible whether each equation is true or false. The article reports that "our arithmetic-affective priming may be used as an indirect measure of math anxiety", and suggests it is "a useful tool in establishing the affective value of various arithmetic procedures in different types of math-achieving participants".
requirements: Short stimulus onset asynchrony (250 ms) chosen to influence both retrieval from verbal memory and response selection levels
Participants instructed to ignore the prime word while judging the equation
constraints: The affective value of the target arithmetic problems was initially unknown, so relatedness could not be established as in standard affective priming studies
target_learners: children aged 7 to 13 with and without developmental dyscalculia
target_learning_goals: measuring affective responses to simple arithmetic and math anxiety indirectly
examples: Each participant underwent 160 trials using 40 primes four times each, twice with a true equation and twice with a false equation as target
key_sources: Rubinsten O, Tannock R. (2010). Mathematics anxiety in children with developmental dyscalculia. Behavioral and Brain Functions 6:46. http://www.behavioralandbrainfunctions.com/content/6/1/46

article_title: Collaborative learning through augmented reality role playing
citation: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://education.mit.edu
title: Redesigned AR engine with time dependence, cascading events, and distinct player roles (Charles River City and Mad City Murder)
description: To promote greater collaboration between teams, the authors redesigned their core AR game engine, from which two games were created: Charles River City (CRC), combining environmental science and epidemiology, and Mad City Murder (MCM), a mystery investigation. The engine adds "time dependence, cascading events and distinct player roles." Roles receive different information from virtual characters, have different data collection capabilities, and can exchange information via infrared beaming — for example, a detective must beam information about an ill student to a nurse so she can interview and examine symptoms.
requirements: Roles must have distinct information access and data collection capabilities, and devices must support infrared beaming of information between players
constraints: Role overlap must be balanced: too much overlap removes positive interdependence and individual accountability, while too little overlap does not give students enough common ground to discuss the problem space
examples: In one CRC version, three roles — doctor, environmental scientist, and department of public health expert — each had unique data access, and students beamed and radioed information across teams
key_sources: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://doi.org/10.3115/1149293.1149333

article_title: Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency
citation: Zhou X, Wei W, Zhang Y, Cui J, and Chen C (2015) Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency. Front. Psychol. 6:1364. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01364
title: Arithmetic intervention should consider targeting visual perceptual processing
description: Based on the finding that visual perceptual ability accounts for the numerosity–fluency relation, the authors recommend that interventions for mathematical learning difficulty consider visual perceptual processing as a target, rather than focusing solely on non-symbolic quantity processing. They state: "Our results suggest that arithmetic intervention should consider targeting visual perceptual processing." They draw a parallel to reading intervention where action video game play improved reading speed, most likely due to enhanced visual attention.
requirements: Interventions should be designed for children whose arithmetic difficulties may stem from visual perceptual processing rather than magnitude processing deficits
constraints: The recommendation is based on correlational and regression evidence, not on a tested intervention
key_sources: Zhou X, Wei W, Zhang Y, Cui J, and Chen C (2015) Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency. Front. Psychol. 6:1364. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01364

article_title: The CSCL field matures
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). The CSCL field matures. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 5:1–3. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9077-5
title: Journal article length should be just enough to clearly express and support the claims, and no longer
description: The editors state that the main consideration for article length is having "something important to say, a significant contribution to the field," and that "the length should be just enough to clearly express and support the claims — and no longer." They note most past articles averaged about twenty formatted journal pages, while remaining open to shorter formats and occasional longer articles when the content requires it.
requirements: The article must have something important to say — a significant contribution to the field — before length is considered
constraints: The editors remain open to shorter articles (book reviews, notes, reports) and to occasional longer articles when a complex framework or thorough review requires lengthy motivation, presentation, and illustration
target_learners: CSCL researchers and authors submitting to ijCSCL
target_learning_goals: Academic writing and publication in the learning sciences
examples: In this issue, one paper presents a complex framework requiring lengthy presentation and another reviews an extensive realm of CSCL research with impressive thoroughness; neither strikes the editors as verbose
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). The CSCL field matures. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 5:1–3. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9077-5

article_title: Traversing planes of learning
citation: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7
title: Artifacts as bridges: affordances that open up connections between planes
description: The article develops an account, drawing on Heidegger's analysis of bridges and Bonderup Dohn's affordances, in which artifacts "afford" connecting levels: "A highway ramp or bridge often creates a possibility that did not otherwise exist for going from one level to another at a given point". The connecting is not accidental but belongs to the artifact's nature and design, which opens up a shared world. This supports a post-cognitive shift away from individual-mind-centered analysis toward how language, tools and resources work.
requirements: Resources must be identifiable units of the physical world, including speech and gesture, involved in meaning-making practices
constraints: The account is framed as a helpful physical analogy for conceptual connections between levels of learning, not a model or explanation
target_learning_goals: meaning-making and knowledge building mediated by artifacts and resources
examples: Heidegger's analysis of the Alte Brücke of Heidelberg, and the I-90 bridge ramps across the Hudson River, serve as the physical illustrations
key_sources: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7

article_title: Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection
citation: Iordanou, K. (2022). Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 399–425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09289-1
title: Reflection sheets prompting reflection on one's own dialog transcript during argumentation
description: Reflection sheets (adapted from Iordanou & Constantinou, 2015) supported experimental-condition participants in reflecting on the electronic transcript of their own dialog while waiting for the opposing pair to respond. "Own-side reflection sheets asked participants to reflect on (a) whether they had paid attention and addressed the opposing side's position, and (b) whether they had used evidence in the counterarguments they had constructed". Other-side reflection sheets asked participants to reflect on the rebuttals they used to weaken counterarguments to their own position and whether they used evidence to support their rebuttal; in both cases participants contemplated what a better counterargument or rebuttal might have been. Participants worked with a same-side collaborating partner to promote externalization of thinking.
requirements: An immediately available and permanent record of the dialog (the electronic transcript) as the basis for the reflective activity; a collaborating same-side partner
constraints: The sheets alternated across sessions and were used during Sessions 5–9 only in the experimental condition
target_learning_goals: meta-strategic and epistemic awareness of argumentation goals: addressing the opponent's position and using evidence
examples: During Sessions 5–9, A&R participants completed alternating own-side and other-side reflection sheets on chosen excerpts of their instant-messaging dialogs
key_sources: Iordanou, K. (2022). Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 399–425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09289-1

article_title: Incoming Editor’s Editorial
citation: Fred Paas. (2015). Incoming Editor's Editorial. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9347-x
title: Journal articles in educational psychology should be clear and accessible for educational practice as well as rigorous
description: The incoming editor states a quality expectation for contributions to EDPR: articles should not stop at rigor but should also communicate in terms usable by practitioners. He writes that it is important that articles "not only emphasize theoretical and methodological rigor but also are clear and accessible for educational practice." This principle applies across all the article types the journal accepts.
requirements: Articles must meet theoretical and methodological rigor standards while remaining clear and accessible for educational practice.
target_learners: Educational psychology researchers and education practitioners reading journal articles
target_learning_goals: Communicating research findings so they can inform educational practice
examples: The editor applies this expectation to all submissions to the EDPR portal, whether reviews, meta-analyses, intervention studies, replications, essays, interviews, commentaries, or reflections.
key_sources: Fred Paas. (2015). Incoming Editor's Editorial. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9347-x

article_title: Effects of School-led Greenspace Interventions on Mental, Physical and Social Wellbeing in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review
citation: Vi Ly · Dianne A. Vella-Brodrick. (2024). Effects of School-led Greenspace Interventions on Mental, Physical and Social Wellbeing in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09963-1
title: Attention Restoration Theory and Stress Reduction Theory explain nature's restorative effects on wellbeing
description: The review presents two complementary theories for the human–nature connection. Attention Restoration Theory "posits that exposure to nature provides a restorative effect by recovering directed (effortful) attention after prolonged mental activity", with restorative settings requiring being away, extent, and compatibility. Stress Reduction Theory "proposes that natural environments have a restorative effect that reduces physiological stress and negative emotions" after stressful situations. Together with the Biophilia Hypothesis, they frame why school nature exposure may enhance wellbeing for learning.
requirements: Nature settings must provide fascination, being away, extent, and compatibility to be restorative under ART
constraints: The review notes these theories are frameworks proposed to explain nature–health links, applied here to school settings
target_learning_goals: mental wellbeing supporting optimal learning experiences
examples: The review uses ART and SRT to motivate examining school-led nature interventions on affect, stress, PA and social outcomes

article_title: Exploring the Nature-Creativity Connection Across Different Settings: A Scoping Review
citation: Vella-Brodrick, D. A., Lewis, K. J., & Gilowska, K. (2024). Exploring the Nature-Creativity Connection Across Different Settings: A Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09964-0
title: Attention Restoration Theory and the alternating attention orientation model as explanations for how nature enhances creativity
description: The review presents Attention Restoration Theory (ART; Kaplan) as the most commonly used explanation for how nature's restorative effects indirectly enhance creativity by reducing cognitive fatigue and renewing attention. Under ART, "goal-directed attention is a finite resource" that fatigues, and nature restores it via "soft fascination" — effortless attention held by low-stimulation yet fascinating surroundings, contrasting with absorption-driven hard fascination. The review also describes Williams et al.'s alternating attention orientation model, in which attention alternates between fascinating natural surroundings and inward mind-wandering, both placing low demand on attentional control and potentially strengthening the illumination and evaluation phases of the four-stage creative process.
requirements: Exposure to low-stimulation natural surroundings during or after cognitively demanding preparation, consistent with the incubation phase of the creative process
constraints: The review notes mindfulness and soft fascination are distinct constructs whose exact relationship, and thus their relationship to creativity, remains unclear
target_learners: adults across education, workplace, and arts contexts
examples: The review describes placing nature exposure after the cognitively demanding preparation phase so attention renews while ideas incubate unconsciously

article_title: How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry?
citation: Luciano Gasser · Yvonne Dammert · P. Karen Murphy. (2022). How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry? Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1445–1475. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09667-4
title: Support argumentative peer dialogues that require children to justify perspectives and consider divergent views about narrative fiction
description: From the critical-analytic stance, children learn socially from narrative fiction by engaging in argumentative dialogues that require them to reason for their own perspectives and consider divergent perspectives. Through such dialogues with peers or adults, children learn to justify their interpretation, respectfully listen to others' ideas, critically examine others' arguments, and develop openness toward alternative views. The review positions this stance as going beyond both moral-message extraction and perspective simulation by emphasizing reasoned and justified judgments about complex sociomoral issues.
requirements: Classroom dialogues about narrative fiction need to fulfill specific characteristics if educators aim to promote more than basic sociomoral competences
constraints: Initial expressive responses are a necessary but insufficient condition for intellectual and sociomoral growth and must be expanded by critical reflection
target_learners: children and adolescents in classroom literary discussions
target_learning_goals: social reasoning, critical evaluation of perspectives, and balanced text interpretation
examples: The review describes argumentative dialogues in which children legitimize their own perspectives while considering peers' alternative perspectives on complex sociomoral issues raised in narrative fiction

article_title: Effects of Nature (Greenspace) on Cognitive Functioning in School Children and Adolescents: a Systematic Review
citation: Dianne A. Vella-Brodrick · Krystyna Gilowska. (2022). Effects of Nature (Greenspace) on Cognitive Functioning in School Children and Adolescents: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1217–1254. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09658-5
title: Attention Restoration Theory, Stress Reduction Theory and the Biophilia hypothesis as complementary accounts of nature's cognitive benefits
description: The review organizes underlying mechanisms around three theoretical perspectives, each "a distinctive but complementary explanation for why nature could benefit cognitive functioning". Attention Restoration Theory holds that natural environments elicit "soft fascination" that releases goal-directed attention and permits cognitive restoration; Stress Reduction Theory proposes that physiological stress reduction induced by nature enhances cognition; the Biophilia hypothesis posits an innate drive to affiliate with nature for survival and psychological restoration. The review maps included studies to these frameworks using corresponding measures such as the Perceived Restorativeness Scale, vagal tone and affect scales.
requirements: Studies testing these theories employ corresponding measurement approaches, e.g. perceived restorativeness scales, physiological stress instruments, and eye-tracking for soft fascination
constraints: The review notes Stevenson et al. found no significant difference on executive attention, which is central to ART, and that van den Berg et al. provided no additional support for ART
examples: Amicone et al.'s studies reported higher Perceived Restorativeness Scale scores for natural than built environments; Stevenson et al. used mobile eye-tracking and found more eye fixations per minute in nature, which the authors linked to soft fascination

article_title: Measuring arithmetic: A psychometric approach to understanding formatting effects and domain specificity.
citation: Rhodes Katherine T., Branum-Martin Lee, Washington Julie A., Fuchs Lynn S. (2017). Measuring arithmetic: A psychometric approach to understanding formatting effects and domain specificity. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000189
title: Arithmetic assessment and intervention should account for problem format and the role of executive attention and language, not treat all arithmetic scores as measures of one ability
description: Because formatting affects what arithmetic measures tap, the article argues that scores from differently formatted arithmetic items should not be interpreted interchangeably as indicators of one math ability. It concludes that "in addition to arithmetic-focused interventions, interventions targeting executive attention, language, and/or the interplay between them (i.e., internal speech during problem-solving) may be a promising avenues of mathematical problem-solving intervention." This principle follows from the finding that executive attention directly predicted all arithmetic outcomes while language contributed only to language-formatted items.
requirements: Assessment batteries must measure arithmetic in multiple formats alongside language and executive attention measures so that construct contributions can be separated.
constraints: The intervention implication is stated prospectively by the authors as promising, not tested in this study, which used only baseline data.
target_learning_goals: arithmetic problem-solving and valid measurement of mathematical ability
examples: The study assessed 1,314 third graders with 11 arithmetic measures spanning language-formatted word problems, Arabic numeral computation, and estimation tasks, plus language and executive attention batteries.

article_title: States of epistemic curiosity interfere with memory for incidental scholastic facts
citation: Keller, N. E., Salvi, C., Leiker, E. K., Gruber, M. J. & Dunsmoor, J. E. (2024). States of epistemic curiosity interfere with memory for incidental scholastic facts. npj Science of Learning 9:22. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00234-w
title: Arousal-biased competition account of curiosity's overshadowing of nearby scholastic information
description: The article interprets its findings through an arousal-biased competition model of memory allocation, in which the goal-state to resolve uncertainty about a high-curiosity trivia question competes with and overshadows encoding of other material presented close in time. The authors write that "arousal will enhance memory when there is need for selective attention toward the target information", and that arousal "can narrow the focus of attention toward stimuli that are irrelevant to the source of arousal". Because the trivia and scholastic material share a similar epistemic nature, bottom-up pop-out of incidental items may be blunted, reversing the spillover benefit seen for simple visual stimuli.
requirements: A phasic high-curiosity state elicited by specific target material, and unrelated material presented in close temporal proximity to it
constraints: The article applies the account to trial-by-trial, second-scale phasic curiosity states, not to sustained tonic curiosity
The overlap between arousal generally and curiosity specifically is, per the authors, an open question meriting further investigation
target_learning_goals: retention of complex scholastic facts (science, history, English) presented near curiosity-eliciting material
examples: The three task versions presented the scholastic fact before or after the trivia answer, and in all versions high-curiosity pairing impaired scholastic memory

article_title: Improving analytical reasoning and argument understanding: a quasi-experimental field study of argument visualization
citation: Simon Cullen, Judith Fan, Eva van der Brugge and Adam Elga (2018). Improving analytical reasoning and argument understanding: a quasi-experimental field study of argument visualization. npj Science of Learning 3:21. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0038-5
title: Argument visualization: tree diagrams exposing the logical structure of argumentative texts
description: Argument visualizations are tree diagrams that illustrate the logical relations in argumentative text. "Claims, the sentences contained in white boxes, are the fundamental units of argument visualizations", grouped beneath horizontal green brackets labeled "because" (reasons, which aim to raise confidence in a conclusion) or red brackets labeled "however" (objections). Their "hierarchical layout is intended to re ﬂect the hierarchical structure of real arguments", with color and grouping cues binding elements that share a common function; dashed borders mark premises that remain implicit in the text. In the seminar, students produced such visualizations of real scholarly texts as the medium for analysis, discussion, feedback, and revision.
requirements: Training uses real academic texts rather than highly simplified arguments
Timely, detailed, individualized instructor feedback on students' visualizations
Students actively generate their own representations rather than receiving explanations of the readings
constraints: The present findings do not disentangle the contribution of visualization itself from the intensive, interactive course and its explicit focus on argument analysis
target_learners: undergraduate students, primarily first-year students at a selective university
target_learning_goals: parsing argumentative texts into logical components
examples: Students worked in groups of two or three to visualize arguments from contemporary analytic philosophy papers, then revised visualizations in response to weekly feedback before submission
Problem sets began as fill-in-the-blank exercises with progressively less scaffolding before students visualized arguments from scratch

article_title: Non-invasive peripheral nerve stimulation selectively enhances speech category learning in adults
citation: Llanos, F., McHaney, J. R., Schuerman, W. L., Yi, H. G., Leonard, M. K. and Chandrasekaran, B. (2020). Non-invasive peripheral nerve stimulation selectively enhances speech category learning in adults. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0070-0
title: Arousal-based salience-gated neuromodulation account of paired-tVNS speech category learning
description: The article proposes that sub-threshold tVNS engages ascending brainstem neuromodulatory systems, and that "temporally precise changes to arousal can enhance the gain of perceptually salient stimuli, resulting in greater memory consolidation speci ﬁcally for these stimuli." Under arousal-biased competition (ABC) and GANE models, arousal benefits perceptually salient stimuli and not less salient ones, explaining why stimulation paired with the more salient easier-to-learn tones (cued by pitch height, a dominant dimension for English listeners) enhanced learning while hard-category pairing did not. The account is consistent with the null FFR findings, locating the effect in attention/arousal-modulated consolidation rather than sensory re-encoding.
requirements: Stimulation must be temporally paired with the to-be-learned stimuli so the arousal signal is precise rather than diffuse.
constraints: The article states the null FFR result may reflect the approximately 25 min session being too short to drive sensory plasticity, or sub-threshold intensities being suboptimal for this modality.
The article states it cannot directly link invasive cervical VNS in animal models to auricular tVNS in humans, and stimulation frequency was not manipulated.
target_learners: Adult native English speakers learning non-native speech categories
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of non-native speech sound categories (Mandarin tone categories)
examples: Stimulation paired with easier-to-learn Tone 1/3 enhanced learning while pairing with harder-to-learn Tone 2/4 did not, matching the salience-gated prediction.

article_title: High-intensity acute exercise impacts motor learning in healthy older adults
citation: Eleanor M. Taylor, Claire J. Cadwallader, Dylan Curtin, Trevor T.-J. Chong, Joshua J. Hendrikse & James P. Coxon. (2024). High-intensity acute exercise impacts motor learning in healthy older adults. npj Science of Learning 9:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00220-2
title: U-shaped arousal and dose-response intensity account for exercise effects on motor learning in older adults
description: The article offers an explanatory account in which acute exercise benefits motor learning depend on intensity and task cognitive demands. It notes the arousal–cognition relationship "is thought to be U-shaped" so higher intensity may harm complex cognition, while a dose-response relationship favours higher intensity for consolidation, possibly via catecholamines, lactate, and BDNF. This framework organises why exercise hurt acquisition yet preserved retention in older adults.
requirements: Exercise intensity and timing must be characterised relative to the learning task's cognitive demands
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation; the study tested only one high-intensity protocol immediately before learning in older adults
examples: The study used a 20-minute HIIT protocol reaching up to 90% HRR, contrasting with moderate-intensity protocols in prior older-adult studies that found no behavioural effect

Tracking of user interaction history to individualize questions

article_title: Improving Adaptive Learning Technology through the Use of Response Times
citation: Everett Mettler, Christine M. Massey, Philip J. Kellman. (2011). Improving Adaptive Learning Technology through the Use of Response Times. Proceedings of the 33rd Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society. https://cognitivesciencesociety.org
title: ARTS: Adaptive Response Time Based Sequencing
description: ARTS is an adaptive learning system that uses response times along with accuracy as primary inputs to govern adaptive sequencing. All items receive priority scores updated after every trial as a function of learner accuracy and RTs, trials elapsed, and predetermined mastery criteria; retention intervals expand as an inverse function of response time, so faster accurate responses automatically produce longer recurrence intervals. The system implements rapid reappearance of missed items via a priority increment W, interleaving via an enforced delay constant D, dynamic spacing based on a log function of RT, and retirement criteria requiring several consecutive fast correct responses. The article states the algorithm "may utilize any equations relating elapsed time or trials, accuracy, and RT to the priority for presentation of an item."
requirements: Interactive learning trials that record both accuracy and response time for each item
Adjustable parameters (a, b, r, W, D) set to suit particular learning contexts and even individual learners
constraints: Model-based alternatives such as Atkinson's system require pre-programming of learning parameters based on data from a prior learning experiment, whereas ARTS requires no prior study
RTs for inaccurately answered items are not considered meaningful
target_learning_goals: factual knowledge such as geography and multiplication facts
examples: In Experiment 1, ARTS trained participants until each item was answered correctly three times in a row under 10 sec per item, retiring items as criteria were reached
In Experiment 2, the Best Basic Math program used mastery strips to indicate overall progress and gave feedback on each trial and for 10-trial blocks

description: A set of four researcher-developed Arabic CBM assessment tools for early literacy: Letter Naming Fluency, Letter Sound Fluency, Phoneme Segmentation Fluency, and Word Reading Fluency. examples: LNF sheets display 28 Arabic letters with a one-minute limit (average correlation between versions .96); WRF sheets contain 76 Arabic words ranging from 2 to 6 letters (average correlation .80).

citation: Hadida Barzilai Dor, Tejman‐Yarden Shai, Yogev David, Vazhgovsky Oliana, Nagar Netanel, Sasson Lior, Sion‐Sarid Racheli, Parmet Yisrael, Goldfarb Abraham, Ilan Ophir. (2024). Augmented Reality‐Guided Mastoidectomy Simulation: A Randomized Controlled Trial Assessing Surgical Proficiency. The Laryngoscope. https://doi.org/10.1002/lary.31791
title: AR‐guided 3D‐printed temporal bone mastoidectomy training system (HoloLens with QR‐code auto‐registration)
description: A training system combining a 3D‐printed PLA temporal bone model with Microsoft HoloLens 2 augmented reality. A CT scan is segmented with D2P software, printed, and labelled with a "10 × 10 QR code" on a flat frame surface; the model hologram is projected via D2P and registration is achieved by the QR code, with "estimated drift of less than 2‐3 mm". HoloLens auto‐registration runs continuously during drilling so the hologram stays fixed on the moving model, overlaying structures such as the sigmoid sinus, facial nerve, and semicircular canals.
requirements: A printed 3D model with a QR code on a flat surface for registration, and the D2P software plus Microsoft HoloLens 2 platform
constraints: The PLA model does not mimic the haptic feedback of drilling a human temporal bone, has uniform colors that do not replicate natural tissue shades, and does not integrate with an operating microscope
target_learners: medical students in their clinical clerkship
examples: Twenty‐one clerkship students drilled the model once, with the AR group receiving dynamic overlays of critical structures during drilling

article_title: The Effect of Passive and Active Education Methods Applied in Repetition Activities on the Retention of Anatomical Knowledge.
citation: Kooloos Jan G.M., Bergman Esther M., Scheffers Marieke A.G.P., Schepens-Franke Annelieke N., Vorstenbosch Marc A.T.M. (2020). The Effect of Passive and Active Education Methods Applied in Repetition Activities on the Retention of Anatomical Knowledge. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.1924
title: Memory-based account of why active learning was expected to aid repetition: arousal, schemas, and retrieval
description: The article frames repetition effects with a three-process memory account: information is encoded into working memory, stored in long-term memory schemas built from new and existing information, and retrieved. It states that "Active learning methods try to arouse the learner by giving them the opportunity to control the information that is experienced," and that arousal helps construct stronger, larger schemas that ease retrieval. The study's hypothesis that active repetition methods would outperform passive ones derived from this account, but the results did not confirm it.
requirements: The account assumes previously learned knowledge exists in schemas that can be reactivated by retrieval cues such as attention and arousal
constraints: The article notes it "seems to be unknown what a necessary degree of attention should be for the retrieval of information from schemas"
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and retrieval of previously learned knowledge
examples: The authors propose that all three repetition conditions offered enough attention and arousal cues — a teacher recalling material, an e-learning module with questions, or peer explanations — making passive methods "good enough" for retrieval

description: The AR Magic Mirror is a screen-based augmented reality system "employing the mirror metaphor", in which users see a reflection of themselves with virtual anatomical information superimposed on a large display. article_title: PBL and sustainable education: addressing the problem of isolation.
citation: Noordegraaf-Eelens, L., Kloeg, J., & Noordzij, G. (2019). PBL and sustainable education: addressing the problem of isolation. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 24(5), 971-979. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09927-z
title: Arendt's vita activa framework (labor, work, action) as a lens for reconnecting PBL to a shared world
description: The article introduces Hannah Arendt's distinction among three modes of human activity: "labor, work, and action". Labor meets immediate needs with a circular structure; work is goal-oriented, fabricating objects of permanence and fashioning the shared human world; action introduces something new into the world ("natality") and creates institutions. The authors use this nested framework to diagnose PBL's threefold isolation and to argue for cultivating responsibility for a shared world as the basis of sustainable education.
requirements: Education should equip students with skills and practical knowledge contributing to common sense and responsibility for a shared world, without replicating actual job situations in the tutorial
constraints: Action cannot be fully defined without a separate scholarly discussion; the article focuses only on its importance to education
target_learners: higher education students in PBL programmes
